The Princess Bride

The Princess Bride is thirty-nine years old and people still quote it at weddings.

Full analysis below
Film · Theatrical June 7, 2026 Analyzed by Debra Ducane 12 min read
Woke Score

✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

The Princess Bride does not qualify as a woke trap under any reading of VVWS v1.1. The film's margin is +18 TRAD. The only woke-adjacent element is the corrupt aristocracy as villain, which is genre-standard for fairy tale adventure and carries no hidden ideological payload. The film is exactly what it presents itself as: a swashbuckling love story with adventure, honor, and the purest possible declaration that true love conquers all. Nothing is hidden. Nothing arrives late to subvert the apparent premise.

Our Verdict on The Princess Bride

The Princess Bride is thirty-nine years old and people still quote it at weddings.

'As you wish.' 'Inconceivable!' 'My name is Inigo Montoya. You killed my father. Prepare to die.' 'True love is the greatest thing in the world, except for a nice MLT.' 'Have fun storming the castle.' 'Death cannot stop true love. All it can do is delay it for a while.'

The lines have become part of the language. This does not happen with average movies. It happens with films that capture something true about how people want to live and love.

The premise is a grandfather reading a fairy tale to his sick grandson. The grandson protests: 'Has it got any sports in it?' The grandfather replies: 'Are you kidding? Fencing, fighting, torture, revenge, giants, monsters, chases, escapes, true love, miracles.' The grandson is eventually convinced. So is everyone who watches.

Westley loves Buttercup. He goes to sea to earn a fortune so they can marry. He is captured by the Dread Pirate Roberts and presumed dead. Buttercup, believing him gone, agrees to marry the loathsome Prince Humperdinck, ruler of Florin. She is kidnapped by a trio of remarkably incompetent criminals. Westley, who has become the new Dread Pirate Roberts, rescues her. The film's last act involves storming a castle, defeating a six-fingered man, and disrupting a wedding.

None of this is played straight. All of it is meant. The Princess Bride understands something about storytelling that most films forget: you can be in on the joke and still feel the emotion. You can wink at the camera during the sword fight and still hold your breath during the torture scene. The humor does not undercut the stakes. It is part of why the stakes feel safe to invest in.

The film's traditional credentials require almost no argument. Westley's love for Buttercup is the kind of love that does not compute in modern romantic storytelling. He does not question whether she is worth it. He does not weigh his options. He crosses an ocean, becomes a pirate legend, and fights his way through a castle for a woman he loves. His competence is moral as much as physical. He is the best swordsman in the world, the best climber, the best strategist, and none of it matters to him except as tools for getting Buttercup back.

Inigo Montoya is the film's other great traditional figure. His entire life has been organized around a single honorable purpose: avenge his father's murder. He is the most memorable secondary character in the film because Mandy Patinkin plays him with complete earnestness inside the comedy. Inigo is not a joke. He is a man who has kept a promise to a dead father for twenty years and finally gets to keep it. His moment of victory is one of the most emotionally satisfying scenes in the film. 'I want my father back, you son of a bitch.' The line lands because the film has earned it.

Fezzik is the gentlest giant in film history. He rhymes because it helps him think. He is loyal to Inigo through everything. He carries people when they cannot walk. His friendship with Inigo is built on love and history and a genuine delight in each other's company. There is no agenda in their relationship. They are friends, and the film shows you what that looks like.

The villains are worth noting. Humperdinck is a coward who wants war for political reasons. Count Rugen is a sadist who studies pain with academic detachment. Both are aristocrats. The film does position corrupt nobility as the opposition. But this is fairy tale logic, not political programming. The villain is the prince because princes are the villains in fairy tales. The film is not making an argument about hereditary aristocracy as a system. It is using the oldest storytelling grammar in the Western tradition.

Rob Reiner is, in the real world, one of Hollywood's most aggressive liberal activists. Reviewing this film honestly requires setting that aside, because The Princess Bride contains none of his personal politics. He served William Goldman's story. Goldman's story is about true love, honor, courage, and keeping your promises to the dead. These are traditional values.

The grandfather-grandson framing is the film's final traditional gift. The grandfather reads to his sick grandson, and by the end the grandson is completely won over. He asks the grandfather to come back tomorrow and read it again. The grandfather says: 'As you wish.' The oldest story structure in the world: an elder passing a story to the young, and the young receiving it. That is what The Princess Bride is doing, and it is doing it in plain sight.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Rob Reiner

WOKE. Reiner is one of Hollywood's most outspoken liberal political activists. He co-founded the I Am Love consortium, has made explicitly political documentary films, and is one of the most vocal anti-conservative voices in the entertainment industry. None of this is hidden or ambiguous. However, The Princess Bride was made in 1987, before the current culture war framework existed, and it was adapted faithfully from Goldman's 1973 novel. The film's ideology is Goldman's, not Reiner's. Reiner's political views did not infect the adaptation. His craft served the material. This is a consistent pattern in film history: directors with strong political views often make their most enduring work when they subordinate those views to a great story.

Rob Reiner directed some of the best American films of the 1980s and early 1990s. This Is Spinal Tap (1984). Stand by Me (1986). The Princess Bride (1987). When Harry Met Sally (1989). Misery (1990). A Few Good Men (1992). The Shawshank Redemption (1994, as producer). This is an extraordinary run of quality. He has said that The Princess Bride was the most difficult film of his career to get made because no one in Hollywood believed the book could be adapted. Goldman had turned down previous offers for years. When Reiner finally got the rights, he worked with Goldman on the screenplay directly. The result is one of the most faithful book-to-screen adaptations in Hollywood history. As a director, Reiner served Goldman. As a political activist in the decades since, Reiner has been consistently left-liberal. These are two separate things.

Content Breakdown

Adult Viewer Insight

What makes The Princess Bride hold up for adults who have seen it twenty times is Goldman's understanding of the relationship between irony and sincerity. The film knows it is a fairy tale and says so directly. It winks at its own conventions. And then it plays those conventions completely straight anyway, because it knows that the conventions exist for a reason. True love is a cliche because it is real. Honor is a cliche because it matters. A man who crosses an ocean for the woman he loves is a stock figure because that is what love looks like when it is serious. Goldman does not deconstruct the fairy tale. He tells it as well as it can be told and trusts the audience to feel why it works. Adults who grew up with this film are adults who learned from it what a story can do when it respects its audience.

Parental Guidance

Rated PG. Appropriate for ages eight and up. Sword fights throughout, none graphic. Giant rat creatures in the Fire Swamp. A torture device that is brief and not explicit. Westley is 'mostly dead' temporarily. The humor and warmth of the film make even its darker moments feel safe. One of the better family films for watching with children old enough to follow a story.
